extraction.name: LAMBADA
extraction.description: LAMBADA (LAnguage Modeling Broadened to Account for Discourse Aspects) is a dataset to evaluate the capabilities of computational models for text understanding by means of a word prediction task. It is a collection of narrative passages sharing the characteristic that human subjects are able to guess their last word if they are exposed to the whole passage, but not if they only see the last sentence preceding the target word. The dataset consists of 10,022 passages, divided into 4,869 development and 5,153 test passages, extracted from novels in the Book Corpus.
extraction.creator: Denis Paperno, Germán Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bernardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, Raquel Fernández
extraction.citeAs: Paperno, D., Kruszewski, G., Lazaridou, A., Pham, Q. N., Bernardi, R., Pezzelle, S., Baroni, M., Boleda, G., & Fernández, R. (2016). The LAMBADA dataset: Word prediction requiring a broad discourse context. In Proceedings of the 54th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (pp. 1525-1534).
extraction.rai:dataCollection: LAMBADA passages were sourced from the Book Corpus (unpublished novels). After duplicate removal and filtering of offensive material, the corpus contains 5,325 novels and 465 million words. Novels were randomly divided into equally-sized training and development+testing partitions. Passages were filtered to exclude those easily guessable by standard language models (a pre-trained RNN, a 4-gram model, a RNN trained on Book Corpus, and a feed-forward model). Any passage whose target word had probability >= 0.00175 according to any of these language models was excluded. Remaining passages were evaluated by human subjects through CrowdFlower in three steps: (1) one subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage; (2) if correct, a second subject guessed based on the whole passage; (3) if both correct, more subjects (up to 10) tried to guess based on the target sentence only. If no subject could guess from the sentence alone, the passage was added to LAMBADA.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Document analysis, Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The Book Corpus (Zhu et al., 2015), consisting of unpublished novels. After duplicate removal and filtering of potentially offensive material with a stop word list, the corpus contains 5,325 novels and 465 million words.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Duplicate removal and filtering out of potentially offensive material using a stop word list. Novels were randomly divided into training and development+testing partitions. Passages were formed by extracting target sentences (final sentence) with a context of minimum number of complete sentences before the target sentence such that they cumulatively contain at least 50 tokens. Passages easily guessable by standard language models (target word probability >= 0.00175) were filtered out.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human subjects on CrowdFlower evaluated passages in three steps: (1) one subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage; if correct, (2) a second subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage; if also correct, (3) additional subjects tried to guess the target word based on the target sentence only, with up to 10 unsuccessful guesses allowed, each subject given 3 guesses per sentence. If no subject was able to guess the target word from sentence only, the passage was added to LAMBADA. The same subject could not judge the same item in both passage and sentence conditions.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Strict hit-or-miss approach requiring perfect match: two consecutive subjects had to exactly match the missing word, and no subject (out of up to 10) could provide it from local context alone, even when given 3 guesses. In the crowdsourcing pipeline, 84-86% items were discarded at step 1, an additional 6-7% at step 2 and another 3-5% at step 3. Only about one in 25 input examples passed all selection steps.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: At least 2 annotators for passage-level guessing (steps 1-2), and up to 10 annotators for sentence-level guessing (step 3).
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: English speakers recruited via CrowdFlower crowdsourcing service.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Pre-trained recurrent neural network (Mikolov et al., 2011), standard 4-gram model, RNN trained on Book Corpus, feed-forward model (for filtering passages).
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The development set of LAMBADA, along with the training corpus, is available at http://clic.cimec.unitn.it/lambada/. The test set was to be made available at the time of a planned public competition.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Strong bias toward proper nouns (48% of target words), followed by common nouns (37%) and verbs (7.7%). Proper nouns are hugely over-represented compared to the POS distribution in the input. The dataset contains significantly more direct speech (71% of items) than the input sample (61%). More than 80% of LAMBADA passages include the target word in the context.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset uses strict perfect-match criteria, potentially excluding passages with valid alternative continuations. The criteria make the task inherently difficult for standard language models (by design, passages easily guessable by simple language models were filtered out). LAMBADA is intended as a tool to evaluate general-purpose models for broad-context understanding, not as a resource to develop ad-hoc models. Cost considerations limited the number of subjects used at stage 1.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Testing and evaluation of language models on their ability to take a broad discourse context into account when predicting a word. The training data (203 million words from 2,662 novels) can be used for training language models, the development set can be used to fine-tune models to the specifics of LAMBADA passages, and the test set is used for evaluation.
